title: Mark One Cell, Read Its Family

scenes.tts: A stain shows what a cell is now. It cannot follow descendants. A birth date marks one cohort of cells. A lineage is one family: all the descendants of one cell. Could one embryonic cell make many cell types, or did the population hold many committed ones? Population grafts could not tell.
scenes.visual: Mixed row of cells of four shapes (a stain shows each one now); a dashed arrow with a question mark for the descendants a stain cannot follow; a cohort ringed, then one cell fanning to a whole family; then two rival origins (one cell, many types; many committed cells) leading to the same mix, with a question mark.

scenes.tts: One route is to watch. Brenner chose a small transparent worm whose cells could be watched alive. Sulston watched living worms and recorded which cell divided into which. Another is to inject a tracer into one identified cell. Its descendants receive it in active form. A large dextran tracer cannot pass to neighbours, so only descendants carry it.
scenes.visual: Left: a viewing ring, a cell divides and a lineage tree is drawn. Right: a pipette injects an orange tracer into one cell of a row; it divides, both daughters orange, neighbours not; a blocked arrow shows the dextran cannot pass.

scenes.tts: A retrovirus joins its genome to a dividing cell's DNA, so every descendant inherits the insert. A Cree reporter puts a fluorescent protein gene behind a stop flanked by lox P sites. Cree deletes the stop, so the reporter is read in that cell and all its descendants. Fuse Cree to a mutated estrogen receptor domain, and tamoxifen switches it on. A low dose marks few, scattered cells.
scenes.visual: Three columns. Retrovirus: an insert joins a cell's DNA and both daughters carry it. Reporter: a stop-bar shutters the reporter lamp between two lox sites; Cre removes it and the lamp lights, then the daughters light. Inducible: Cre fused to an estrogen-receptor domain is dim until tamoxifen arrives; a low dose lights a few scattered cells in a sheet.

A low dose marks few, scattered cells.

scenes.tts: Colour can separate neighbours. Brainbow chooses at random among three or more fluorescent proteins, and combinations from tandem copies gave about ninety colours. Confetti switches on one of four, so neighbouring clones can differ in colour. Weinreb and colleagues gave blood progenitors barcodes expressed as R N A and passed to every descendant. McKenna and colleagues used Cas nine target arrays that gather mutations, so shared patterns reveal relatedness.
scenes.visual: Left: grey cells take random colours from many; then four colours with neighbouring patches differing. Right: a cell with a barcode divides, every descendant carries it; a lineage with a mutation that appears in a branch and is shared by its descendants.
scenes.caption: Colour can separate neighbours. Brainbow chooses at random among three or more fluorescent proteins, and combinations from tandem copies gave about 90 colours. Confetti switches on one of four, so neighbouring clones can differ in colour. Weinreb and colleagues gave blood progenitors barcodes expressed as RNA and passed to every descendant. McKenna and colleagues used Cas9 target arrays that gather mutations, so shared patterns reveal relatedness.

scenes.tts: Mark cells sparsely, and a cluster is read as one progenitor's family. That is a sampling argument, not an observation. In the gut, Snippert and colleagues used four colours. Some clones grew while others vanished, and crypts drifted toward one colour over one to six months. This fits neutral drift among equivalent stem cells. With N of them, one clone takes over a crypt with probability one over N.
scenes.visual: Top: a sparse sheet with one orange cluster ringed as one family. Bottom, marked idealised example: rings of stem cells in four colours at start, later, and 1 to 6 months, ending in one colour; the 1/N rule.

With N of them, one clone takes over a crypt with probability 1/N.

scenes.tts: Two neighbouring cells marked at once look like one clone, so keep induction sparse and count close pairs of marks. Leaky labelling: in the 1996 test no excision appeared in untreated animals, yet a 2020 mouse study found labelling without tamoxifen in every CreERT2 line it examined, more with some reporters than others. So give full-genotype animals vehicle, and check the reporter stays off.
scenes.visual: Left: two adjacent marked cells grow into one merged cluster, one clone or two; green controls. Right: an untreated sheet with stray marked cells; 1996 test none seen, later work some; green control with vehicle.

scenes.tts: In 1988, Bronner-Fraser and Fraser injected dye into single chick dorsal neural tube cells. Many clones held several cell types, so some crest cells are multipotent before leaving the tube. That needed single-cell marking. In 2010, Ginhoux and colleagues pulsed tamoxifen. Adult mouse microglia derive from primitive myeloid progenitors that arise before embryonic day 8, not significantly from postnatal blood progenitors. That needed a pulse in time.
scenes.visual: Left: a neural tube, dye into one dorsal cell, clone of several cell types, tag Bronner-Fraser and Fraser 1988. Right: timeline with embryonic day 8, primitive myeloid progenitors marked by a tamoxifen pulse leading to adult microglia, postnatal blood progenitors crossed, tag Ginhoux 2010.

scenes.tts: In 2019, Shi and colleagues marked scattered cambium cells in Arabidopsis, using dexamethasone as the inducer, not tamoxifen. Of ninety-nine clones at ten days, thirty-five spanned xylem, cambium and phloem. This is read as support for one bifacial stem cell. A cluster read as one family is a sampling argument, not an observation.
scenes.visual: Plant layers xylem, cambium, phloem: one marked cambium cell; a clone spanning all three; a grid of 99 clones with 35 lit; tag Shi 2019; then the rule in a box.
